en: 1.1 Fundamentals of Human Computer Interaction Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) defines the fundamental design of technology to serve people. It refers to systems that are easy to use, efficient, and responsive to human needs. HCI is also known as CHI (Computer-Human Interface) or MMI (Man-Machine Interaction). Sensory Channels of Interaction Humans and computers communicate by using the following sensory channels: Channel How Humans Use It How Computers Respond Sight ( ) Look at screens, graphics, or videos. Displays visuals on monitors/screens. Touch ( ) Tap, type, or swipe. Responds with clicks or vibrations (Haptics). Hearing ( ) Listen to sounds or voices. Provides audio feedback via speakers. Voice ( ) Speak commands (e.g., "Alexa"). Processes speech and replies. Spatial ( ) Move in physical space. Tracks position or body movement (e.g., VR). HUMAN Sight Touch Hearing Voice

en: Traditional vs Natural Interaction 1.1.1 Traditional Interaction Refers to the basic way people use everyday devices. It relies on standard input and output methods. Computer: Moving a mouse and typing on a keyboard. Output via monitor and speakers. Smartphone: Tapping and swiping on a touchscreen. Output via screen lighting and vibrations. 1.1.2 Natural Interaction Refers to advanced, smart technology that allows people to interact without a mouse or keyboard. It feels more human. Voice: Speaking commands into a device (e.g., "Alexa, play a song"). Body & Gesture: Facial recognition to unlock a phone, or playing VR games by waving hands. 👨‍🏫 Class Discussion Ask students to list 3 traditional interfaces they used today (e.g., TV remote, ATM keypad) and 3 natural interfaces (e.g., FaceID, Siri, Kinect Games).

en: 1.2 Applications of HCI ★ GOLDEN TOPIC The applications of HCI extend to the design and development of interactive systems such as desktop applications, websites, and mobile apps. These are human-centered solutions built to meet user needs across diverse domains. Domain Application Examples User Benefit Health Care Patient portals, telemedicine apps, assistive technologies. Improves access to medical services remotely. Banking Mobile banking apps, secure ATM interfaces. Enables quick transactions and secure financial management. Education E-learning platforms (LMS), online exam portals. Enhances teaching, learning, and student engagement. Networking & Communication Social media platforms, messaging apps (WhatsApp), Zoom. Connects people globally through collaboration tools. HCI Networking Education Healthcare Banking

en: 1.3 Components of HCI Human-Computer Interaction relies on several primary components that work together. i) User ( ) Any individual or group that interacts with a computer system to achieve defined goals. Classified into two categories: 1. End Users: Individuals who directly operate the system (from beginners to experts). 2. Stakeholders: People/groups with an interest in the system's outcome (managers, clients). ii) Computer System ( ) The platform where humans and computers communicate through input, output, and feedback using an interface. It connects human actions with machine responses. iii) User Interaction ( ) The process through which a user communicates with a system by performing actions (clicking, tapping, typing, speaking). It transforms user intent into system responses. (Types detailed on next page). iv) Task ( ) The specific action users perform (e.g., booking a ticket). Characteristics include: Task Complexity: Difficulty level (filling a form vs designing a 3D model). User Knowledge: Skills required (basic typing vs advanced programming). Time Requirement: Duration needed (ATM withdrawal vs online passport application).

en: Types of User Interaction User interaction can happen in many different ways depending on the technology used. Interaction Type Description Examples Direct Manipulation Handling digital objects on a screen exactly like physical objects. Dragging files, zooming images with fingers. Command-Based Giving precise instructions through typed text commands. MS-DOS, Linux Terminal (dir, cd..). Menu-Driven Selecting from predefined lists or options instead of typing. Clicking "Start Test" or "Download" on a portal. Form Fill Entering structured data into blank text fields. Sign-up forms, ticket booking screens. Conversational Communicating with systems using natural human language (text/voice). Chatbots, ChatGPT, Google Assistant.

en: Types of User Interaction (Continued) Interaction Type Description Examples Gesture-Based Using body or hand movements to control systems. Swiping touchscreens, VR hand gestures. Voice Interaction Speaking commands directly to the system. "Call Aslam" on a smartphone. Context-Aware Systems sense the environment and act automatically without prompt. Smart lighting turning on when entering a room. Biometric Using biological features for interaction and authentication. Fingerprint unlock, Facial recognition (FaceID). Haptic & Tactile Providing physical feedback to confirm actions. Phone vibration when typing. Multimodal Combining two or more interaction types together. Voice + touch (speaking a search, then tapping).

en: Interfaces, Environment & Feedback v) User Interface (UI) The medium through which humans interact with computer systems. Graphical User Interface (GUI): Uses visual elements like windows, icons, and menus (e.g., Windows OS, Android). Command-Line Interface (CLI): Uses text-based typing (e.g., MS-DOS, Linux Terminal). Touch Interface: Interaction via gestures like tapping, swiping, pinching (e.g., Smartphones, Tablets). Voice User Interface (VUI): Interacting through spoken commands (e.g., Smart Speakers). Natural User Interface (NUI): Relies on gestures, body movements, or immersive environments (e.g., VR Headsets, Microsoft Kinect). vi) Environment The real-world setting where a person uses a computer system. It is shaped by physical conditions (e.g., an ATM outdoors in sunlight), social conditions (e.g., a quiet classroom), and technical hardware. vii) Feedback The signal or response given to confirm or guide actions. System Feedback Response from the computer (e.g., "Loading..." bar, "Message Sent!" tick mark, or an Error sound). User Feedback Input from the user to the system (e.g., tapping a "Submit" button, giving a 5-star rating).

en: 1.4 Importance of HCI ★ GOLDEN TOPIC HCI ensures that machines are approachable and usable, turning complex technology into everyday tools. Good design makes technology simple and enjoyable (e.g., touchscreens). Poor design causes confusion and risks (e.g., unclear buttons on medical devices). Important Implications of HCI: Implication Description 1. Enhance Productivity Well-designed interfaces help users work faster, make fewer mistakes, and achieve goals efficiently. 2. Promotes Inclusivity Accessibility features (screen readers, voice commands) empower marginalized groups and ensure equal use of technology for everyone. 3. Drives Innovation Emerging tech like AR/VR, AI, and IoT rely strictly on solid HCI principles for people to actually adopt and use them. 4. Economic Impact User-friendly products gain higher adoption rates, customer loyalty, and market success, driving profits. 5. Ethical Responsibility Responsible design ensures technology respects user privacy, reduces bias, and supports human well-being.
